paragraphs.title: The Persecuted Person’s Cry and Sense of Distance from God

answers: In the daytime and in the night season
easy.explanation: He says, “I cry in the daytime” and “in the night season.”
easy.q: When does the speaker cry unto God?

easy.explanation: The speaker says, “But thou art holy.”
easy.q: How is God described in the passage?

easy.explanation: He cries continually and says that God does not answer him.
easy.q: What does the speaker lack despite crying out?

medium.explanation: He asks why God is far from helping him and says, “thou hearest not.”
medium.q: Why does the speaker feel that God is far away?

medium.explanation: The phrase shows that the speaker continues to call upon God through the night.
medium.q: What does the KJV phrase “am not silent” mean in context?

medium.explanation: Even while lamenting, he addresses God as holy.
medium.q: To whom does the speaker continue to turn despite feeling forsaken?

answers: The speaker is silent while God speaks
The speaker feels forsaken but continues praying
The speaker is joyful but complains
challenge.explanation: He feels far from God, yet he continues to cry unto Him day and night.
challenge.q: What central tension appears in this passage?

answers: The speaker prays only at one time
challenge.explanation: Day and night together emphasize persistent prayer and unrelieved distress.
challenge.q: What does the repeated mention of day and night emphasize?

answers: It denies the value of prayer
It preserves reverence and faith amid lament
It identifies God as an enemy
challenge.explanation: The speaker’s complaint remains directed toward the holy God who dwells among Israel’s praises.
challenge.q: How does the description of God as holy shape the passage?

paragraphs.title: The Ancestors’ Deliverance and the Speaker’s Humiliation

easy.explanation: The passage says, “Our fathers trusted in thee.”
easy.q: In whom did the speaker’s fathers trust?

answers: As a worm and no man
easy.explanation: He says, “I am a worm, and no man.”
easy.q: How does the speaker describe himself?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “All they that see me laugh me to scorn.”
easy.q: How do those who see him respond?

answers: The fathers trusted and were delivered, while he is despised
The fathers feared, while he conquered
The fathers were silent, while he refused to pray
medium.explanation: The fathers trusted in God and were delivered, but the speaker describes humiliation and rejection.
medium.q: What contrast does the speaker make between the fathers and himself?

answers: An object of shame or disgrace
medium.explanation: A reproach is someone treated with shame, blame, or contempt.
medium.q: What does “a reproach of men” mean?

medium.explanation: He says God took him from the womb and was his God from his mother’s belly.
medium.q: What lifelong relationship does the speaker remember after describing his humiliation?

answers: It highlights the contrast between their rescue and his present suffering
It proves that he is not part of Israel
It shows that he no longer believes in God
challenge.explanation: The speaker remembers past deliverance while experiencing a very different condition.
challenge.q: Why is the deliverance of the fathers important while the speaker is being mocked?

answers: He moves from public humiliation to remembered divine support
He claims he never received help
challenge.explanation: After describing how others despise him, he recalls God’s care throughout his life.
challenge.q: What does the movement from “a worm” to God’s care from birth suggest?

challenge.explanation: These gestures accompany the people’s scorn and ridicule.
challenge.q: What do the lip-shooting and head-shaking of the onlookers express?

answers: Trouble is near and there is none to help
easy.explanation: He says, “trouble is near; for there is none to help.”
easy.q: Why does the speaker ask for help?

easy.explanation: The passage mentions bulls, a ravening lion, and dogs.

answers: They divide his garments and cast lots for his vesture
easy.explanation: They “part” his garments and “cast lots” upon his vesture.
easy.q: What do the enemies do with the speaker’s clothing?

answers: As being poured out like water and having strength dried up
medium.explanation: He says, “I am poured out like water” and “My strength is dried up.”
medium.q: How does the speaker describe his physical weakness?

answers: His inner strength is melting away
medium.explanation: The image describes severe inner collapse and weakness.
medium.q: What does it mean that his heart is “like wax”?

answers: Their encirclement increases his danger and weakness
They have no connection with his suffering
medium.explanation: The surrounding enemies accompany his physical and emotional collapse.
medium.q: How are the enemies connected to the speaker’s condition?

answers: The number and threatening power of the enemies
challenge.explanation: The animal images portray enemies surrounding and threatening him from every side.
challenge.q: What do the images of bulls, a lion, and dogs emphasize?

answers: They assume the speaker’s defeat is certain
They expect the speaker to escape
They are asking him for forgiveness
challenge.explanation: Casting lots for his clothing suggests that they regard his situation as hopeless.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the enemies dividing the garments during the crisis?

answers: Only the body is described as strong
Only the spirit is described as joyful
challenge.explanation: Bones, heart, strength, tongue, and the dust of death all convey total collapse.
challenge.q: How do body and spirit work together in this description of distress?

easy.explanation: He says, “Be not thou far from me, O LORD.”
easy.q: To whom does the speaker address his request for help?

easy.explanation: He mentions the sword, the dog, the lion, and the horns of the unicorns.
easy.q: From what does the speaker ask to be delivered?

easy.explanation: He says, “O my strength, haste thee to help me.”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask God to do quickly?

medium.explanation: He directly calls God, “O my strength.”
medium.q: How does the speaker describe God in this plea?

medium.explanation: The phrase is an urgent request for God to come quickly to his aid.

answers: The speaker is surrounded by dangers and has no other helper
He has nothing more to say
medium.explanation: The sword, dog, lion, and wild oxen represent immediate and overwhelming threats.
medium.q: Why is the request especially urgent?

answers: His prayer becomes shorter, direct, and urgent
challenge.explanation: Commands such as “Be not thou far,” “Deliver,” and “Save me” create urgency.
challenge.q: How does the speaker’s style change in this passage?

answers: He feels threatened from every direction
He is in a secure place
challenge.explanation: The sword, dog, lion, and horns create a picture of danger on every side.
challenge.q: What does the variety of dangers reveal about the speaker’s state?

answers: The speaker sees God as the only sufficient source of help
God is counted among the enemies
The speaker no longer needs rescue
challenge.explanation: Calling God his strength explains why he urgently asks Him for deliverance.
challenge.q: Why is the title “my strength” fitting in this prayer?

paragraphs.title: Thanksgiving and Salvation in the Congregation

answers: Declare God’s name and praise Him
easy.explanation: He says, “I will declare thy name” and “in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee.”
easy.q: What does the speaker promise to do after deliverance?

answers: The seed of Jacob and the seed of Israel
easy.explanation: He addresses all the seed of Jacob and Israel.
easy.q: Whom does the speaker call to glorify the LORD?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “The meek shall eat and be satisfied.”
easy.q: Who shall eat and be satisfied?

answers: God did not despise the afflicted and heard his cry
God hid His face from the afflicted
The afflicted never cried to God
medium.explanation: The speaker says God did not despise the afflicted and heard him when he cried.
medium.q: Why does the speaker call the congregation to praise God?

medium.explanation: The phrase says that God did not reject or loathe the suffering of the afflicted.
medium.q: What does “despised nor abhorred” mean in context?

answers: Deliverance leads to worship, satisfaction, and renewed life
The meal prevents the congregation from praising
medium.explanation: The passage moves from praise in the congregation to the meek eating, being satisfied, and living.
medium.q: How are praise and eating connected in the passage?

answers: A change from distress to thanksgiving after God’s hearing and deliverance
That he has forgotten his former suffering
challenge.explanation: The speaker who cried in affliction now promises public praise.
challenge.q: What does the movement from crying to praise show?

answers: The deliverance becomes a public testimony
The speaker wants to conceal the deliverance
He has nothing personal to say
challenge.explanation: Public praise allows the congregation to hear of God’s faithfulness and join in worship.
challenge.q: Why is the praise offered “in the midst of the congregation”?

answers: Enduring life and encouragement for those who seek the LORD
A desire to flee from God
challenge.explanation: The phrase expresses lasting hope and renewed life for the worshipers.
challenge.q: What hope is expressed by “your heart shall live for ever”?

paragraphs.title: God’s Kingship over the World and the Generations

answers: The ends of the world and the kindreds of the nations
easy.explanation: The passage says that all the ends of the world and all the kindreds of the nations will worship.
easy.q: Who will turn unto the LORD and worship before Him?

easy.explanation: It says, “For the kingdom is the LORD’S.”
easy.q: To whom does the kingdom belong?

answers: God’s righteousness and what He has done
That the speaker’s garments were divided
easy.explanation: The final verse says they shall declare His righteousness and that He has done this.

answers: The kingdom and government belong to Him
They want to escape from Him
medium.explanation: The passage grounds their worship in the LORD’s kingship and rule among the nations.
medium.q: Why will the nations worship before the LORD?

answers: The farthest parts of the earth
A place beside the sea only
medium.explanation: The phrase refers broadly to the distant regions of the whole world.
medium.q: What does “all the ends of the world” mean?

answers: From the speaker’s deliverance to the nations and future generations
From the world to one enemy only
From the congregation to the speaker alone
medium.explanation: The vision moves from personal praise to worldwide worship and generational testimony.
medium.q: How does the salvation described here expand?

answers: The salvation becomes a reason for the whole world to acknowledge God’s rule
The salvation causes people to deny God’s kingdom
challenge.explanation: God’s saving work leads the nations to remember, turn, and worship because He is King.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between salvation and God’s kingship?

answers: The message of God’s righteousness is meant to continue into the future
The message belongs only to the speaker
challenge.explanation: The passage says that a people yet to be born will hear and declare what God has done.
challenge.q: What does the mention of future generations imply?

answers: The focus moves from personal lament to universal praise and kingship
The focus moves from praise to abandonment
The focus moves from worldwide worship to complete silence
challenge.explanation: The psalm develops from an individual cry of abandonment into a vision of worldwide worship and enduring testimony.
challenge.q: What major movement occurs between the beginning and end of the psalm?
